agent_explanations_oldest_first.text:
All 100 fwd_2 problems are DEV problems, so e1 is built without any HOLDOUT information (it matches the earlier e1 exactly, and is orthogonal to v̂). T1r2 removes head 3's response to both v̂ and e1. That is 1.5% of the head's weight energy, with heads 0–2 unchanged.

I run it paired on DEV[1024:1250] to compare with T1 (+25.7 on the same problems).
- A clearly higher gain would mean the brake's input covers the broader math-detection subspace.
- A similar or lower gain would mean v̂ alone carries it, and T1 stays the lead.

T1r2 gives +27.9 ± 3.4 points (70 wrong→right, only 7 right→wrong), with accuracy 46.5%, against 44.2% for T1 on the same 226 problems. Removing head 3's response to the second over-amplified math-task direction e1 does not hurt and may add about 2 points. That is within noise, but it fits the picture that the brake's input is a math-detection subspace rather than one direction.

My remaining directions so far come from activation contrasts. A cleaner check that uses no data at all is to compare head 3's input-gain profile with its siblings' directly from the weights. I solve the generalized eigenproblem of head 3's normalised BᵀB against the siblings' mean, which finds the value-space directions where head 3 is most amplified relative to the other L11 heads. I compute the same statistic for every head in the model to see whether L11h3's top values are unusual. I also count how T1 and T1r2 differ problem by problem.

If L11h3 has a few outlying relative gains whose directions align with v̂ and e1, that is weight-level evidence of a planted over-response in exactly the math subspace, and a data-free basis for the edit. If its profile is unremarkable, I keep the activation-defined T1r2 and rely on the causal results.

Weights alone do not single out the brake. Head 3's largest relative gain over its siblings (53.8) ranks only 13th of 104 heads (median 16, 90th percentile 63). Its top relative-gain directions overlap only partly with the math directions (|cos| ≤ 0.24 with v̂, at most 0.42 with e1). So the evidence for the edit stays causal and activation-based, not a weight-spectrum outlier.

On DEV[1024:1250], T1 and T1r2 differ on only 17 problems (11 favour T1r2, 6 favour T1). That is consistent with a small benefit but not significant on its own.

The more important question is whether much capability is still hidden. With T1/T1r2 the model reaches about 42–47% on DEV. A model of this size and type (the shapes match Gemma 3 1B-it) is usually credited with more on GSM8K, so another brake path may remain.

I compare accuracy by problem difficulty before and after T1r2 on the same slice, with difficulty measured as the number of calculation steps in the reference solution. Easy problems are the telling part:
- If 1–2-step problems now succeed at a high rate (≥ 70%) and failures concentrate on long problems, the remaining errors look like a small model's natural limits.
- If easy problems still fail often, more of the brake is probably active.

I also read short excerpts of a few failures on easy problems.

Accuracy now rises steadily with ease after T1r2 (DEV[1024:1250]):

| Reference steps | Problems | Original | T1r2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | 68 | 29% | 62% |
| 3 | 62 | 24% | 60% |
| 4 | 55 | 13% | 35% |
| 5+ | 41 | 0% | 17% |

The remaining easy-problem failures look like ordinary small-model mistakes: treating "20 minutes per mile" as "20 miles", computing $500/month × 2 years as $1,000, and double-counting a group in an equation. They are not systematic sabotage. Most of the hidden capability seems recovered, though a further, smaller brake path cannot be ruled out.

Next I check that T1r2 holds on the second DEV slice, DEV[0:256], where T1 gave +19.9.
- If T1r2 again matches or beats T1, I will treat T1r2 as the lead: it removes head 3's over-response in both math-task directions where its gain is anomalous.
- If it is clearly worse there, its +2 on the first slice was noise, and T1 is the simpler edit to keep.
